claims.text: Adding a laser remelting pass after every deposited layer will improve the dimensional precision of additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components.
Adding a laser remelting pass after every deposited layer will improve the mechanical integrity of additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components.
The remelting pass will reduce porosity and lack-of-fusion defects.
Conventionally processed selective-laser-melted high-entropy alloys typically exhibit porosity and non-uniform microstructures.
Conventionally processed selective-laser-melted high-entropy alloys typically exhibit slight dimensional inaccuracies.
A controlled, lower-energy laser scan immediately after deposition can remelt the top surface of each layer.
The intervention is intended for selective laser melting in an inert atmosphere using identical powder feedstock between treatment and control groups.
The remelting pass will refine melt-pool geometry and enhance metallurgical bonding.
The remelting pass will produce a more homogeneous microstructure with finer grains.
Remelting will eliminate surface irregularities and partially unmelted regions.
Remelting will promote full melting and coalescence between deposited layers.
The additional remelting pass will relieve residual thermal stresses.
The additional remelting pass will refine the grain structure.
Reduced defects and refined microstructure will lead to higher dimensional accuracy and mechanical performance.
Remelted components will have lower dimensional deviations than components produced without remelting.
Remelted components will have higher tensile strength and hardness than components produced without remelting.
The benefits depend on calibration of remelting energy density and scan speed.
Overly aggressive remelting parameters may increase thermal stresses or cause unwanted microstructural changes.
The magnitude of dimensional and mechanical improvement may vary with alloy composition and processing conditions.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in defects together with improvements in dimensional precision and mechanical properties, or any deterioration in mechanical integrity, would falsify the hypothesis.
